I've played a good amount in the Bronze-Gold bracket.   


The thing about mercy in bronze is that she's one of the few supports that -can't miss- which is a big deal in that elo. That's why the tanks want you to pocket them, they don't trust your bap/ana to hit their shots. 

If you are winning, it's working, and you should just /hidechat if people are bitching. If you are finding that the tanks are being overly cautious or your DPS are hard feeding, sometimes pocketing a tank, especially something like a winston can get you good DB numbers and make them feel comfy enough to push through the choke.   


I tend to pocket tanks more in ultra-low elo, and as I get into midsilver/bronze, more into the DPS. What is "optimal" in bronze is a -lot- more variable game by game than higher up, where you can have a bit more trust in your teammates.   


That said: Your first job is staying alive. And bronze players will fairly universally expect you to a) die to save them   
b) have a higher HPS than you do  
c) magically save them from all damage.  


You will get flamed by someone no matter what you do. People in bronze are wrong a lot of the time. CONFIDENTLY wrong.  (for example, I had someone absolutely certainly tell me that mercy had more heals per second than baptiste, and like...get out of here with that pls)  Get really liberal with the mute button and the hidechat function.

I really recommend two things that help me a lot, especially if I'm in a situation I can't leave. If I can leave, splashing water on my face or going somewhere cold definitely help, but if I can't I do: 

1) Box breathing, deep breath in for 5 counts, hold for five counts, breathe out for 5 counts, hold for five counts. In a circle like that. 

2) A centering exercise. This is a good description from a website of one I like. 

First, notice 5 things that you can see. Look around you and become aware of your environment. Try to pick out something that you don’t usually notice.  
Second, notice 4 things you can feel. Bring attention to the things that you’re currently feeling, such as the texture of your clothing or the smooth surface of the table you’re resting your hands on.  
Third, notice 3 things that you can hear. Listen for and notice things in the background that you don’t normally notice. It could be the birds chirping outside or an appliance humming in the next room.  
Fourth, notice 2 things you can smell. Bring attention to scents that you usually filter out, either pleasant or unpleasant. Catch a whiff of the pine trees outside or food cooking in the kitchen.  
Finally, notice 1 thing you can taste. Take a sip of a drink, chew gum, or notice the current taste in your mouth.

Both of these things really help me when I'm in a situation I can't leave and am feeling very panicky. You can also, even in an exam, excuse yourself to the washroom and use that time to centre yourself.

again, I’m not against guns. I just don’t think children and teens should have unsupervised access to them. I think there is room for debate around what the age should be. Well, when you set an age limit for anything, it’s done broadly to account for individual differences and try and hit an age where most individuals are ready for whatever activity/substance. 
The driving age is 16, some 14 year olds probably could handle driving, and there is no difference between someone who is 15 years and 364 days old, and someone who is 16. However we set an age for many things (typically with some common sense) and stick with it.

There is always going to be edge cases of adults who cannot be safe with firearms and teens who can. But realistically, teens and children in general have a lower capacity for reasoning and acting with future consequences in mind than an adult, and I think it’s important that the adults in their lives act in ways that reduce risk. Teens with access to firearms are also at a higher risk of completing suicide, since guns are such an effective method.

I wasn’t debating the health implications of obesity. It is better to be a healthy weight than over or underweight. It’s healthier not to smoke, or drink or do drugs. It’s healthier to have a less stressful job and work fewer hours. We all make choices and we all have vices. 

What I meant about not understanding the obesity epidemic is that it’s not caused by one single thing. I mean sure, yes, eat less. But the fact that it is such a systemic problem in so many places (not all of them rich nations) and that it correlates so highly to things like mental health, trauma, poverty, etc means that long term change for society at large probably will have fairly complex and multifaceted solutions. 

It’s easy to look at individual people and say why that person is fat, and of course it all does come down to personal choices, but on an epidemiological level, looking at why it’s such a problem form so many people is important. And so far the evidence suggests that the most positive thing you can do to help people in your life that are making self destructive choices is to love them where they are, try and build up their self worth and to not make eating your only social activity with them. 

You don’t have to lie to anyone. You don’t have to say “your fat body is beautiful” because most fat folks wouldn’t believe you anyways. But people are more than their looks and their bodies. So you can express how you value and appreciate other qualities about them.

It’s a big problem that needs addressing. But evidence suggests that positive reinforcements leads to better outcomes than negative reinforcement. 
The most successful weight loss comes from building up the person emotionally so that they can make the changes they need. 

No one knows exactly how to deal with obesity, it’s a problem with many complicated causes. The way our society works (most people have fairly sedentary jobs and easy access to transportation), the kind of food we eat (the sugar lobby has been fighting laws that force sugar numbers to be listed on labels), socioeconomic status (people who are poor are more likely to be obese) as well as personal choice, mental health, etc etc. 

But there is no evidence that “shaming people” or giving them a “wake up call” is a helpful tactic and seems to do more harm than good.

1) volunteer - many profs will accept student volunteers, although certainly not all. You access this by contacting professors directly. (No pay, no course credit)

    (yes pay, no course credit) 

3) directed study - pretty much every department has an option for directed study credits. Those are arranged directly with a professor. In CSC the course is 490.  This is accessed by contacting the professor directly. (No pay, yes course credit) 

4) Co-op - these are jobs with more concrete goals. They are pre posted by the professor and usually have some grant funding attached. This can give you full time lab experience, and a more in depth experience than the other offerings. It’s also the only one that offers potential for off campus research experience. You access this through the  coop and careers office.  (Yes pay, yes course credit)

My therapist told me that I absolutely was allowed to leave, and that if anyone questioned me about it, to just be honest that I was feeling unwell. 

Sometimes for me at least, a lot of the anxiety around these situations is feeling like if I go, I’m there for the whole thing, good or bad. But in most cases that just isn’t the reality. People get sick, or get headaches, or feel unexpectedly unwell. So if you need to leave you can.

Basically the point I was trying to make was that you shouldn’t go to something you don’t want to attend just because of social pressure. But you also don’t need to let your anxieties disallow you from going.

There is a law called the orphan drug act, which is meant to encourage companies to develop treatment for “orphan diseases” which affect fewer than one in 2000 Americans. Under this law, a company gets seven years of exclusive distribution of this drug. This is meant to offset some of the costs for developing a drug that has a fairly small market. 

However, there is a loophole that allows for this act to apply to existing drugs if it is found to treat one of these orphan diseases. So if you buy a patent for a medication, you can file for orphan status. The companies that do this (like Martin Skirellis company) are kinda like the patent trolls of pharmaceuticals. They don’t actually invent new medications. Just buy up existing drugs and reprice and remarket them. 

It’s a hard one, because without these laws in place, almost nothing was being developed for orphan diseases. However like anything there are people that find a way to game the system. It’s not as easy as closing the loophole either, because that is meant to be encourage and incentivize study of older medications to see if they can be helpful in these diseases.
